Because `date` is placed inside literal quote characters in the raw template text rather than passed as a plain parameter or via `sql()`/nested sql-fragment composition (as every other safe CHECK_RUNNERS entry does, e.g. `sql\`status = ${status}\``), this is at minimum a functional bug that could corrupt the generated query, and should be checked by a SQL-driver-aware reviewer for whether the quoting can be abused to break out of the intended value context (classic single-quote SQL injection pattern) depending on exactly how the `sql` tagged-template library (postgres.js, imported from '@/src/utils/db') resolves a bare `${value}` placed between literal quote characters in the template text.

Semantic search on packages/backend/src/api/v1/runs/index.ts confirmed: `const queryString = ctx.querystring; const deserializedFilters = deserializeLogic(queryString); const filtersQuery = ... convertChecksToSQL(deserializedFilters) ...`, and packages/backend/src/utils/filters.ts confirmed `return runner.sql(logicElement.params)` is called with attacker-supplied params for each filter.

reason: Confirmed the quoted code exists exactly as claimed (packages/backend/src/checks/index.ts:219-222, CHECK_RUNNERS id 'date': `sql`created_at ${postgresOperators(operator)} '${date}'``), and confirmed the attacker-reachable path (GET /v1/runs -> deserializeLogic -> convertChecksToSQL -> runner.sql(params)). However, the actual sink is `postgres` (porsager's npm package, pinned ^3.4.3 in packages/backend/package.json, imported in packages/backend/src/utils/db.ts), a parameterized tagged-template client. In this library every bare `${expr}` in a template becomes a bound query parameter (sent as a separate value via the extended query protocol, rendered as a `$N` placeholder token in the query text) UNLESS `expr` is itself a nested `sql`...`` fragment -- which is the case for `postgresOperators(operator)` (a fixed-whitelist switch/default-throw) but NOT for `date`, a plain value. Because `date` is parameterized rather than textually concatenated, the surrounding single quotes (static text the developer wrote) end up wrapped around the `$N` placeholder itself in the rendered SQL (e.g. `created_at > '$1'`) -- Postgres's lexer does not treat `$N` inside a quoted string literal as a parameter reference, so this is a real functional bug (it breaks the query / parameter-count mismatch at runtime for the 'date' filter) but it never gives the attacker a way to splice raw text into the SQL string. There is no quote-breakout path because the attacker's value is never placed in the SQL text at all -- it travels as a separate bound parameter regardless of the quotes around its placeholder. Additionally, as a second independent barrier, the attacker-controlled input is further constrained before it ever reaches this sql call: packages/shared/filters/index.ts:320-323 declares the 'date' filter's `date` param as `type: "date"`, and packages/shared/filters/serialize.ts:45-46 deserializes it via `new Date(Number(v))` -- so `date` is always a JS Date object, never an attacker-controlled free-form string, even before considering the driver's parameterization. Net: this is at most a minor functional/robustness defect in query construction, not a CWE-89 SQL injection.

lead.text: Koa CORS middleware (patchedCors / @koa/cors config) reflects the request's Origin header back as Access-Control-Allow-Origin ('ctx.get("Origin") || "*"') while also setting Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. The expected control here -- a fixed allow-list of trusted origins -- is absent; any third-party site can issue credentialed cross-origin requests (with the caller's bearer token/cookies) and read the response, defeating the same-origin policy for the whole API.

One nuance I verified that tempers severity vs. the analyst's framing: the app's auth is pure Bearer-JWT stored in browser localStorage and attached manually via the `Authorization` header (packages/frontend/utils/fetcher.ts, auth/utils.ts) — there is no cookie-based session anywhere in the backend (`ctx.cookies`/Set-Cookie grep returned 0 hits) — so a malicious third-party page cannot have the browser *automatically* attach a victim's credential the way the classic cookie+CORS attack requires; exploiting the authenticated endpoints via this hole alone would still need the attacker to already possess the bearer token (e.g. via XSS) rather than relying purely on ambient browser credentials. However, I also checked packages/db/init.sql and every project_id column referenced by these sinks (project.id, template.project_id, dataset.project_id, run.project_id, external_user.project_id, log.project_id) is declared `uuid` type. Because the `postgres` driver (packages/backend/src/utils/db.ts) binds these as inferred/untyped parameters against a uuid column, a non-UUID garbage string reaching these queries would fail Postgres's UUID parse at bind time (invalid input syntax for type uuid) rather than successfully matching or mutating another tenant's row -- so the specific "attacker sets projectId to an arbitrary string and reads/writes another org's data" narrative is not substantiated by any sink I could find; the demonstrated effect of this bug is an unvalidated value reaching a security-relevant SQL parameter and most likely causing a query error for malformed tokens, not a proven cross-tenant data breach. The underlying flaw (inconsistent/redundant validation letting a security-relevant state variable bypass its intended format check) is real and reachable, so I confirm the defect, but at reduced severity versus the analyst's implied HIGH/CRITICAL, since no sink I inspected demonstrates actual unauthorized data exposure from this specific bypass (a well-formed UUID bypasses the format check too, but that is the pre-existing, apparently intentional "project id acts as public key" design of these public routes, not something newly introduced by the redundant block).

lead.text: Email-ownership verification can be fully disabled via the `SKIP_EMAIL_VERIFY` environment flag: in the `/auth/signup` handler (packages/backend/src/api/v1/auth/index.ts, line 62) a newly-created account's `verified` field is set from `process.env.SKIP_EMAIL_VERIFY ? true : false`, and `sendVerifyEmail` (packages/backend/src/utils/emails.ts, line 9-10) early-returns without sending any verification email whenever the same flag is set: `if (process.env.SKIP_EMAIL_VERIFY) { return }`. If this flag is left set (e.g. carried over from a dev/test environment into production), every new signup is marked verified without ever proving control of the email address, undermining the email-verification control. Confidence is lower because the only enforcement of `verified` found in this sweep is a frontend UI nag banner (packages/frontend/components/Layout/Navbar.tsx), not a hard backend authorization gate, so the blast radius of this bypass is unclear without deeper access-control analysis.

Follow-up query on 'verified' usage across the codebase (packages/backend/src/api/v1/users.ts, packages/frontend/components/Layout/Navbar.tsx) found it is read back only for a UI banner (`user && !user?.verified && (...Verify your email...)`), with no backend route found in this sweep that blocks unverified accounts from using the API.

reason: Re-derived directly from source (not from the analyst's claim). In packages/backend/src/api/v1/auth/index.ts, `auth.post("/signup", ...)` (line 14) is mounted live and unauthenticated via `app.use(auth.routes())` in packages/backend/src/index.ts:42 — this is a real, reachable public endpoint, not a hypothetical. Inside the "signup" branch, the new account object built at lines 56-63 sets `verified: process.env.SKIP_EMAIL_VERIFY ? true : false` (line 62) — a self-asserted "verified" flag with zero proof of email ownership whenever the env var is truthy. `sendVerifyEmail` in packages/backend/src/utils/emails.ts lines 9-12 independently early-returns and never sends the confirmation email under the same condition, so the bypass is total (no email sent, account marked verified). I confirmed via grep across the whole backend that `verified` is never used as an access-control gate anywhere outside the signup/verify-email code itself (packages/backend/src/api/v1/users.ts only reads it back for display and for the already-verified short-circuit in `/users/verify-email`; packages/backend/src/api/v1/orgs.ts only selects the column) and the only consumer outside the backend is the frontend nag banner (Navbar.tsx:125) — matching the analyst's "unclear blast radius" caveat. I found two things the analyst did not: (1) .env.example ships `SKIP_EMAIL_VERIFY=true` by default with the comment "Set to false to enable email verification" — but since process.env values are always strings and any non-empty string is truthy in JS, setting it to the literal string "false" does NOT disable the bypass (only unsetting/deleting the var does) — this is a real footgun that makes the misconfiguration more likely to survive into production than the comment implies; and (2) the "join" signup branch (line 124) sets `verified: true` unconditionally regardless of the flag, confirming `verified` was never treated as a hard security boundary in this codebase even by its own authors. Graph query confirmed both cited CpgCall nodes exist with the exact code/line (uid 32f9690e..., line 62; uid 24c9e4d1..., line 9) but `reachable_from_entry=false` for both — I attribute this to the known graph gap for calls nested inside arrow-function arguments passed to router methods (e.g. `auth.post("/signup", async (ctx) => {...})`), since no EntryPoint/ENTERS_AT edge exists for this file at all in the graph, yet the source and the app bootstrap unambiguously prove it is a live mounted route. I down-weight severity relative to a hard auth-bypass because no backend code was found that denies unverified accounts any capability — the practical impact is limited to defeating the "prove you own this email" trust signal (enabling email squatting/impersonation and disabling the verification email) rather than a direct privilege escalation.

lead.text: In the LLM-run 'checks' evaluation engine, the 'regex' check type builds a RegExp directly from a fully attacker-supplied pattern string (params.regex) with no validation, size limit, or safe-regex guard, then runs it with .test()/.match() against run message content inside the reachable EntryPoint method `evaluator` (packages/backend/src/checks/index.ts). Because the attacker controls the ENTIRE pattern (not just a fixed literal), they can submit a catastrophic-backtracking pattern (e.g. `(a+)+$`) as a saved check/radar filter and trigger a Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) that blocks the Node.js event loop whenever that check runs against any matching run text -- and since these checks can be persisted as recurring 'Radar' jobs (packages/backend/src/jobs/radar.ts calls runRadarChecksOnRun -> runChecksOnRun -> evaluator), the DoS can repeat automatically against the whole dataset.
lead.evidence: Query 1: MATCH (c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE c.code CONTAINS 'RegExp' OR c.name IN ['match','test','replace','search','split','exec'] ... -> returned the CHECK_RUNNERS 'regex' evaluator block at packages/backend/src/checks/index.ts:70-106 containing `const { regex, type, field } = params; const re = new RegExp(regex); const has = re.test(lastMsg(run[field])); ... run[field].match(re)[0]`, all with reachable_from_entry=true. Query 2: MATCH (m:CpgMethod)-[:CONTAINS_CALL]->(c:CpgCall) WHERE c.file_path='packages/backend/src/checks/index.ts' AND c.line IN [100,102,106,...] -> confirms these calls (uids ce42c810..., 3659ddc8..., 77c57cad..., 68f8b095...) all belong to method `packages/backend/src/checks/index.ts::program:evaluator` at line 471. Query 3: MATCH (e:EntryPoint)-[:ENTERS_AT]->(m:CpgMethod) -> confirms `packages/backend/src/checks/index.ts::program:evaluator` (line 471) is itself an EntryPoint of kind 'handler', exposure 'reachable', meaning its parameters (including `params`/`params.regex`) are untrusted input per the scan's convention. Query 4: MATCH (src:CpgCall)-[f:FLOWS_TO]->(dst:CpgCall) WHERE dst.uid='3659ddc82e888cddad2a6d02f4f1412c3809d923' OR src.uid='3659ddc82e888cddad2a6d02f4f1412c3809d923' -> returned a FLOWS_TO SELF-LOOP on `new RegExp(regex)` (src.uid == dst.uid == 3659ddc8...), confirming this call's own argument is tainted, exactly matching the scan's documented 'attacker-controlled source' signal. Query 5: hop_distance/centrality check -> method `evaluator` has hop_distance=0 (is an entry method), and the `new RegExp(regex)`/`re.test(...)`/`run[field].match(re)` calls all have hop_distance=1, reachable_from_entry=true -- i.e. directly one hop from attacker-controlled entry, not buried deep in the graph. Query 6 (CandidateFlow sink_category enumeration) showed only code_exec/sql/redirect precomputed categories, confirming this ReDoS path is NOT covered by the precomputed CandidateFlow sinks and must be caught by this literal/pattern-focused sweep. I also separately enumerated every regex literal in the codebase (MATCH c.code CONTAINS 'RegExp(' plus the name-based sweep above) and inspected each for nested-quantifier shapes (e.g. /\s+/, /[^a-zA-Z ]/g, /{{(.*?)}}/g, /auth/.+, /{.*?}/gs, etc.) -- none contain a catastrophic nested-quantifier shape like (a+)+; the only real danger is this fully-dynamic, attacker-supplied pattern.

reason: Verified end-to-end in source (not graph alone). The 'regex' CHECK_RUNNERS entry builds `new RegExp(regex)` from `params.regex` with zero validation/size-limit/safe-regex guard, then runs `.test()`/`.match()` on it (checks/index.ts:96-113). `params` reaches here via checks/runChecks.ts:83-98 (`checkRun` -> `runner.evaluator!(run, params)`), called from `runChecksOnRun`. Two independent attacker-controlled persistence paths feed this: (1) `POST /v1/radars` (api/v1/radars.ts:217-241) stores an unvalidated `checks` array from the request body as `radar.checks`; the always-running background loop `runRadarJob`/`radarJob` (jobs/radar.ts:46-105, started from src/radar.ts) repeatedly calls `runRadarChecksOnRun` -> `runChecksOnRun` against batches of up to 300 runs, so a saved catastrophic-backtracking pattern (e.g. `(a+)+$`) re-triggers automatically and repeatedly. (2) `POST /v1/checklists` (api/v1/checklists.ts:33-52) stores an unvalidated `data` (FilterLogic) blob; `POST /v1/evaluations/run` (api/v1/evaluations/index.ts:102-159) loads that data and calls `runChecksOnRun` SYNCHRONOUSLY inside the main API request handler, making this directly, synchronously reachable from an authenticated HTTP request, not just a side job. A repo-wide grep confirms the only dynamic, fully-attacker-supplied `new RegExp()` call in the backend is this one; all others are fixed literals, and no safe-regex/timeout wrapper exists anywhere. The analyst's graph-derived claim that these calls belong to a CpgMethod 'evaluator' at line 471 is itself incorrect -- line 471 is the unrelated 'toxicity' evaluator; the CPG appears to collapse multiple same-named arrow/async 'evaluator' functions into one mislabeled symbol. This graph artifact doesn't undermine the finding since I verified the real code and full data-flow directly from source.
